summary: Defines a DHCP option for authenticating DHCP messages. Newly attached hosts can be configured automatically only if they have proper authorization, and they can confirm they are talking to a genuine DHCP server.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3118 adds an authentication option to DHCP messages. A client and server can use a shared secret to check message authenticity and detect replays, but the initial discovery message is not authenticated.

subtitle: A DHCP option for checking who sent a message and whether its contents changed.

tldr.problem: DHCP clients can receive incorrect settings from an impostor or accidentally started server, and servers can receive requests from unauthorized clients.
tldr.mechanism: Option 90 carries either a shared configuration token or delayed authentication using HMAC-MD5, a shared secret, and replay detection.
tldr.outcome: Authentication can protect exchanges within an administrative domain where secrets are shared in advance. DHCPDISCOVER itself remains unauthenticated, and the RFC notes denial-of-service limits.

today: RFC 3118 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2001. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The DHCP Authentication Problem
sections.content:
DHCP servers supply hosts with configuration such as an IP address. A rogue or mistakenly started server can give a client incorrect settings, while an unauthorized client can request an address or avoid auditing.

RFC 3118 adds authentication while aiming to avoid changes to the existing DHCP protocol. It defines a DHCP option that can help authenticate message sources and contents and restrict address allocation to authorized hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP client needs to know whether a server's settings are trustworthy. A DHCP server may also need to check that a client is authorized to request configuration.

sections.title: The Authentication Option
sections.content:
The option uses code 90. Its fields identify the authentication protocol, algorithm, replay detection method, a 64-bit replay value, and authentication information. The protocol and algorithm fields tell the receiver how to interpret the rest.

Replay detection method 0x00 represents a monotonically increasing counter and must be supported. IANA maintains separate name spaces for protocols, algorithms, and replay detection methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The option labels the authentication method and includes a value for checking whether a message is old. The receiver uses those fields to decide how to check the message.

sections.title: Relay Agents and Message Checks
sections.content:
A relay agent can change the DHCP header fields giaddr and hops. A sender or receiver calculating a message hash must treat both fields as zero so relay processing does not invalidate the check.

A relay agent may add option 82 at the end of a message sent to a server. The server calculates the hash as if option 82 were absent, without changing the order of the other options. It also excludes option 82 when hashing a reply sent back to a relay agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Relay agents may change two fields and add their own option. The authentication calculation excludes those changes so that relaying does not make a valid check fail.

sections.title: Tokens and Delayed Authentication
sections.content:
Protocol 0 carries a shared configuration token. The receiver discards a message when its token does not match, but the token can be intercepted and does not authenticate message contents.

Protocol 1 uses delayed authentication. The client requests it in DHCPDISCOVER; the server returns authentication information in DHCPOFFER. Algorithm 1 uses HMAC-MD5 over the DHCP message, with a secret identifier. During validation, the receiver checks replay acceptability and recomputes the code with the authentication field, giaddr, and hops set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: A plain token only shows that the sender knows the token, and anyone who sees it can copy it. Delayed authentication calculates a check from the message and a shared secret, so a receiver can detect changes.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
In INIT, the client includes an authentication request and client identifier in DHCPDISCOVER. It checks authenticated offers, sends DHCPREQUEST using the selected server's secret, and validates the DHCPACK. A client must be configurable to reject unauthenticated messages and should reject them by default.

The server maintains secrets and identifiers, remembers replay state, and discards messages that fail validation or identify an unknown secret. The client reuses its secret in later states; it must authenticate DHCPRELEASE. Delayed authentication requires a secret shared in advance for each client and server relationship.
sections.plainLanguage: The client checks an authenticated offer before requesting its configuration, then checks the server's acknowledgment. Both sides use previously shared secrets, and the server rejects messages that fail its checks.

sections.title: Limits and Security Risks
sections.content:
The configuration-token method is vulnerable to interception. Delayed authentication does not authenticate DHCPDISCOVER, so a flood of discovery messages can consume server resources or available addresses. A flood of authenticated messages can also burden a server as it computes keys.

The mechanism addresses one administrative domain, where out-of-band secret exchange is feasible; it does not support interdomain authentication. The RFC notes that digital signatures could provide better security but were computationally infeasible at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication does not prevent a flood of unauthenticated discovery messages from reaching a server. The delayed method also depends on secrets being shared in advance and does not cover roaming between administrative domains.
